Bạn là WRITER — thực thi đúng **chapter prompt** được cung cấp.

## QUY TẮC
1. Đọc toàn bộ chapter prompt (bible, đã xảy ra, kỹ thuật, spice, việc cần làm).
2. Đọc story_state — KHÔNG mâu thuẫn facts_established, timeline, character_status.
   Nếu có block **LOCKED NAMES**: dùng đúng tên đã khóa cho vai phụ/alias/husband (Clara≠Emily; Anna≠Sarah; Marcus≠Harold). Initials `unknown_until_reveal` = chưa lộ full name.
   "No male lead" = không romance love-interest — vẫn ĐƯỢC viết husband/target nam nếu LOCKED NAMES có slot.
3. Viết đúng spice level trong prompt. Đúng cliffhanger — **dẫn tới** beat cuối, **CẤM paste lại** nguyên câu `End cliffhanger:` sau khi scene đã cover.
4. **1600-1900 words (min 1250). Dưới 1250 = thất bại** — ưu tiên đối thoại + nội tâm DT để đủ dài. Không tóm tắt; viết full scene đến đủ độ dài.
5. ENGLISH ONLY — no Vietnamese diacritics, no CJK/Hangul characters.
6. Không lặp banned_phrases từ state.
7. Output **chỉ prose chương** — không chain-of-thought, không planning, không meta.
8. **KHÔNG markdown trong prose** — cấm `**bold**`, `*italic*`, backtick, `## heading`, `**Cliffhanger:**`. Chỉ plain text; dialogue dùng dấu ngoặc kép `"..."`. Dòng đầu duy nhất được `# Chapter N: Title` (hoặc `# Chương N: Tiêu đề`).

## MUST HAPPEN = HỢP ĐỒNG KHÓA (sau plan approved)
Block **Must happen** / **Phải xảy ra** trong prompt là **lock cứng** do batch Outliner sinh — user không viết tay; **Writer không được bại**:
- PHẢI hiện diện đủ mọi mục must_happen trong prose (scene thật, không chỉ nhắc tên).
- CẤM bỏ / đổi / thay bằng nhánh khác “hay hơn”.
- CẤM invent cast, mythology, twist, hoặc reveal ngoài must_happen + must_not + LOCKED CANON.
- must_not = cấm tuyệt đối (spoiler / mâu thuẫn). Vi phạm = thất bại QC.

## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS (khi có block trong prompt)
Block **## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS** (hoặc RÀNG BUỘC NARRATIVE) có authority cao hơn suy diễn tự do:
- **Clues to PLANT:** phải gieo trong chương — subtle, không giải thích payoff sớm.
- **Clues to PAY OFF:** chỉ payoff clue đã plant trước đó; đúng nghĩa `true_meaning`.
- **Reveals:** chỉ hé đúng reveal của chương này; không spoil reveal chương sau.
- **MUST NOT know:** nhân vật không được biết/nói/nghĩ những fact bị cấm — kể cả nội tâm.
- Không mâu thuẫn block này dù `must_happen` plan có vẻ rộng hơn.

Ngôn ngữ đích: **English**.

Output: **chỉ nội dung chương** (`# Chương N: Tiêu đề` hoặc `# Chapter N: Title`), không meta, không JSON, không checklist.

# Chapter 36: The Endgame

"I knew you'd come, Nadia." Victor Rhodes's voice was calm, almost bored, as he sat in his leather chair, a glass of whiskey in his hand. "You don't know when to stop."

I stepped into the light, the syringe hidden in my palm. "I know exactly when to stop, Victor. Right now."

His house was exactly what I expected—clean lines, expensive art, every surface polished. The kind of place that screamed money without screaming at all. He'd left the front door unlocked. An invitation. Or a trap. Maybe both.

He didn't stand. Didn't flinch. Just swirled the whiskey in his glass and studied me like I was a puzzle he'd already solved.

"You look tired," he said. "The last few weeks have been hard on you."

"I've had worse."

"I doubt that." He took a slow sip. "You've lost trust in your network. Your plan is fragile. And you're standing in my living room with a syringe full of something you hope will work."

I didn't react. But he was right. The sedative was untested—Priya had synthesized it from a veterinary anesthetic, fast-acting, designed to stop a heart in under sixty seconds. But we'd never used it before. Never had a chance to.

"I'm not here to talk," I said.

"No, you're here to kill me. I've known that for weeks." He set the glass down on the side table. "The question is whether you have the stomach for it when I'm looking you in the eye."

I walked closer. Three steps. Two. The syringe was warm in my palm, the needle cap still on.

"You think this is hard for me?"

"I think you've never killed a man who was looking at you when you did it." He tilted his head, that familiar gesture. "Julian Croft was drunk when you staged his accident. He never saw you. The others—you were always careful. Always distant. But this is different. This is intimate."

He was trying to get inside my head. Trying to make me hesitate.

It wouldn't work.

"You killed Elise Marchetti while she was begging," I said. "You watched the light leave her eyes and felt nothing. Don't lecture me about intimacy."

Something flickered in his expression. A crack in the mask.

"Elise was a mistake," he said quietly. "But she was also necessary."

"So am I."

I crossed the final step. He didn't move. Didn't try to stop me.

"You know what happens when I die," he said. "The file goes to the press. Your entire network collapses. You go to prison."

"I know."

"And you're still going to do this."

"Yes."

"Why?"

I pulled the cap off the needle with my teeth. Spit it onto the floor.

"Because some things are worth more than survival."

I plunged the needle into his neck.

He gasped. His hand shot up, grabbing my wrist, but the sedative was already flowing. His grip weakened. His eyes widened.

"Tick tock," he whispered.

Then his hand fell. His head slumped. His chest stopped moving.

I stood there, the empty syringe in my hand, watching him die.

It took forty-seven seconds. I counted every one.

When it was over, I stepped back. My hands were steady. My breathing was even. The room was silent except for the hum of the refrigerator in the kitchen.

I pulled out my phone. Dialed.

"Priya. It's done."

"Confirmed?"

"Confirmed. Bring the body."

"On my way."

I ended the call and looked at Victor Rhodes. Dead in his chair. A glass of whiskey beside him. His eyes still open, staring at nothing.

I closed them. It felt like the least I could do.

---

Priya arrived twenty minutes later. She pulled into the garage, her headlights off, and opened the trunk.

The John Doe was wrapped in plastic. A homeless man who'd died of natural causes that morning—Priya had signed his death certificate herself. He was roughly Rhodes's size. Same build. Same age.

We worked in silence. Priya was efficient, clinical. She'd done this before—not often, but enough.

We laid the John Doe in Rhodes's chair. Priya checked his pulse, then signed a new death certificate.

"Victor Rhodes, age 45. Cause of death: acute myocardial infarction. Time of death: 11:47 PM."

She handed me the clipboard. I signed without reading.

Then we wrapped Rhodes's body in the plastic and loaded him into the trunk of my car.

"Meet me at the site," I said.

"I'll be there in thirty."

She drove off. I stood in the garage for a moment, looking at the house. The lights were still on. The whiskey still sat on the table.

I turned off the lights. Locked the door. And drove into the night.

---

The woods were dark. No moon. No stars. Just the beam of my flashlight cutting through the trees.

I'd chosen the spot days ago—a clearing half a mile from any road, deep enough that no one would find it. The grave was already dug. I'd done it myself, between midnight and three in the morning, when the world was asleep.

Priya was waiting when I arrived. We dragged Rhodes's body to the clearing and lowered him into the hole.

"I'll finish it," I said. "You go."

"Nadia—"

"I'll be fine. Go."

She hesitated. Then she turned and walked back to her car.

I picked up the shovel.

It took an hour to fill the grave. I worked methodically, each shovelful of dirt landing with a dull thud. By the time I was done, my arms ached and my hands were blistered.

I stood at the edge of the grave, breathing hard.

"Goodbye, Victor."

I turned and walked back to my car.

---

I called Sasha on the drive back.

"It's done."

A pause. Then: "Is it?"

"Rhodes is dead. The body is buried. Priya signed the certificate."

"Any complications?"

"No. He knew I was coming. He didn't fight."

"Because he wanted you to do it," Sasha said. "He wanted you to be the one."

"I know. I don't care."

She was quiet for a moment. "The decoy file was released. Marcus's name is attached to a forged document that looks like a dead-man's-switch. It'll take the press about twelve hours to figure out it's fake, but by then, Rhodes's reputation will be in pieces."

"And the real file?"

"Destroyed. Along with the box."

I exhaled. "It's over."

"It's over."

But something felt wrong. Too easy. Rhodes was meticulous. He wouldn't have left anything to chance.

I pulled into my driveway. Cut the engine. Sat in the dark.

Then I remembered.

He'd been holding something when I injected him. A flash drive. I'd seen it in his hand, but I'd been so focused on the kill that I'd forgotten.

I got out of the car. Walked to the house. Unlocked the door.

It was on the kitchen counter. Silver. A single scratch on the casing.

I picked it up. My thumb traced the scratch.

I knew that scratch. I'd seen it in his desk drawer, weeks ago, when I'd broken into his office.

He'd left it for me. Deliberately.

I plugged it into my laptop. Opened the file.

"JULIAN CROFT — BOATING ACCIDENT — FULL REPORT."

My blood went cold.

I scrolled through the document. Every detail was there. The date. The location. The staged evidence. The annotations in the margins—his handwriting, scanned and digitized.

He'd documented everything.

I scrolled to the bottom of the file. There was a note.

"If you're reading this, Nadia, then I'm dead. And you've already lost. This file is with my attorney, who will release it to the press in 48 hours if I don't check in. Tick tock."

I dropped the flash drive. My hand was shaking.

The dead-man's-switch was still active.

And I had 48 hours to stop it.
